_readme: Education Technology library. Fields: type (paper | news | video | example), title, url, source, date (YYYY-MM), blurb, and optionally image/imageAlt (self-hosted under media/), quote, featured (accent card), links [{label,url}]. The page sorts by date, newest first; the blurb must say why the item earns its place, critically and in my voice.

items.title: How can we better identify when a child needs more challenge, or more support?
items.source: Explore Learning at the UK Festival of Education, Wellington College
items.imageAlt: Speaking at the Festival of Education: are pupils learning, or just coping?
items.blurb: Our talk at this year's Festival of Education (2 and 3 July), summarised in this post: the work I lead at Explore Learning on an algorithm for finding each child's optimal zone of proximal development, pairing data science with educator judgement to decide what support, when, and why. We are looking for schools, trusts and research partners to test it with.

items.title: Compass named Adaptive Learning Solution of the Year, 2026 EdTech Breakthrough Awards
items.imageAlt: EdTech Breakthrough Award 2026: Adaptive Learning Solution of the Year
items.quote: We're thrilled to share that Explore Learning's Compass has been named Adaptive Learning Solution of the Year at the 2026 EdTech Breakthrough Awards.
items.blurb: Some context from my side of it. Compass is Explore Learning's adaptive learning platform, and underneath it sits the Aptitude model, which my team and I developed: the machinery that continuously estimates where a child is and what they are ready for next. The award programme drew over 3,000 entries this year, so the recognition says something about the approach, evidence-led modelling paired with expert tutors, rather than just the product. The white paper below sets out the thinking that drove the build.

items.title: The Evidence Imperative: why evidence must come first in AI and children's education
items.source: Explore Learning white paper, written by me
items.blurb: I wrote this for Explore Learning before the Compass work went public. It is a company publication and it carries a marketing narrative in places, I will say that myself. The premise underneath is a valid one, though, and it is the premise that drove the development: personalisation only helps if the system continuously knows the child it claims to support, so put technology where precision and responsiveness pay off, and keep human tutors where judgement and encouragement do. Read it with the UNESCO report in this library as the sceptical counterweight.

items.title: Compass: the smart learning tool behind the award
items.blurb: Included with an obvious declaration of interest: my team builds its models. Compass 2.0 launched in September 2025, places a child's level from around fifteen questions, and forecasts each learner's route to mastery from over half a billion learning interactions. The link explains it in plain terms and the white paper above gives the reasoning; judge it by the standards the rest of this library sets, Bloom's gap, retrieval practice, Freeman's baseline, because that is the bar we hold ourselves to.

items.title: Technology in education: a tool on whose terms?
items.blurb: The most thorough recent stocktake of technology in classrooms, and the most sceptical. I do not accept all of its conclusions, parts of it read as policy positioning, but its central question, on whose terms technology enters the classroom, is one every vendor should be made to answer, myself included. It sits in this library as the counterweight to everything of mine above it.

items.title: The Most Persistent Myth (originally: This Will Revolutionize Education)
items.blurb: Twelve years old and it could have been filmed this morning. Muller walks through a century of technologies that were each going to revolutionise education, film, radio, television, computers, and reaches the conclusion my white paper argues from the other direction: the technology is never the mechanism, the learning relationship is. I keep it here as a test for my own claims. When an AI-in-education pitch cannot say why this time is different, it is this video playing again.

items.title: Active learning increases student performance in science, engineering, and mathematics
items.blurb: A meta-analysis of 225 studies: exam scores rise and failure rates fall when lecturing gives way to active learning. I treat it as the evidential baseline for this whole field. A classroom technology that cannot at least match well-run active learning, a cheap, human, decades-old intervention, is decoration, whatever its demo looks like.

items.title: Test-enhanced learning: taking memory tests improves long-term retention
items.blurb: Retrieval practice: being tested on material beats re-studying it for long-term retention. It is the cheapest, best-replicated effect in the learning sciences, and the first thing I check in any adaptive platform, ours included, is whether its practice is actually retrieval or just re-exposure dressed up as practice. More products fail that check than would admit it.

items.title: PhET Interactive Simulations
items.blurb: Free simulations for physics, maths and chemistry, built, studied and iterated for over two decades. What earns it a place here is the method rather than the product: design around how learners actually explore, measure, revise, repeat. Most of the industry, in a hurry, skips the middle two steps. This is what not skipping them looks like.

items.title: The 2 Sigma Problem: the search for methods of group instruction as effective as one-to-one tutoring
items.blurb: The paper behind almost every pitch for AI tutoring, mine not excepted: tutored students outperforming conventional classes by two standard deviations. I cite it with care. Two sigma was the best case from small studies and later replications land well below it, but even the conservative reading leaves a gap worth building for, and it is the gap adaptive systems are chasing. Read it as a target, not a promise.

items.title: Mind in Society: the development of higher psychological processes
items.blurb: Where the zone of proximal development comes from: the band between what a child can do alone and what they can do with the right help. Chapter 6 is the one to read, and it is striking how directly a 1930s idea specifies what an adaptive learning system should actually optimise. It is the theoretical spine of the algorithm I talked about at the Festival of Education.
